CHAPTER 01 / 16 · THREE WORLDS MEET

Cuba: Where Salsa’s Story Begins

Cuba and the northern Caribbean · October 1492 onward

Salsa’s story begins in Cuba, where Indigenous, Spanish and African cultures came together over centuries. Born out of conquest, slavery, survival and extraordinary creativity, their encounter laid the foundations for some of the world’s most influential music and dances.

In October 1492, Spanish ships reached the coast of Cuba. The island was already home to Indigenous communities with their own languages, music, dances and trading networks. Their encounter with Europe would change the course of Caribbean history.

Spanish conquest began in 1511. Disease, violence and forced labor devastated the Indigenous population. Colonists brought enslaved Africans to Cuba in growing numbers, especially as the plantation economy expanded. Three cultural worlds were now in contact, but under deeply unequal conditions.

Over the centuries, musicians and dancers in Cuba made something new from the traditions they carried and the lives they lived. Indigenous percussion, European instruments and partner dancing, and African rhythms, movement and spiritual traditions all contributed to the island’s musical identity. Salsa itself wouldn’t emerge until much later, in New York. But to understand its music and movement, we have to begin here.

Sources

The sailing ship

The Spanish expedition led by Christopher Columbus reached the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, and Cuba later that month. It opened the way for Spain’s colonization of the Caribbean, bringing European languages, religion, instruments and social customs to the islands. The ship represents the beginning of a long, often violent transformation, not the birth of salsa itself.

Sources
  • Columbus and the Taíno - Library of Congress
  • “The Fairest Island” - Library of Congress

The inhabited coast

Before Europeans arrived, Cuba and its neighboring islands had thriving Indigenous communities. Taíno settlements cultivated crops such as cassava and maintained ties across the Caribbean. The people on this shore had their own cultural histories long before Spanish colonization, and their descendants remain part of Caribbean life today.

Sources
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • Mesoamerica / Caribbean - National Museum of the American Indian
  • Europe Claims America: The Atlantic Joined - Library of Congress

The canoe

The sea connected Caribbean communities rather than simply separating them. Canoes carried travelers, goods and knowledge between islands. Even the word “canoe” comes to English through Spanish from a Taíno word. Like the maracas you’ll meet on the next page, it’s a reminder of the Indigenous legacy in the modern world.

Sources

CHAPTER 02 / 16 · INDIGENOUS CARIBBEAN TRADITIONS

The Taíno: Indigenous Roots

Greater Antilles · Before 1492 and into the present

Long before salsa, the Taíno and other Indigenous Caribbean peoples made music and danced. Their population suffered catastrophic losses after European colonization, but instruments such as the güiro and maracas preserve a legacy you can still hear in Caribbean music today.

The Taíno were among the Indigenous peoples living in Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and neighboring islands when Europeans arrived. Music, dance and storytelling were part of community life. At gatherings known as areítos, people sang and danced to remember their ancestors, leaders and histories.

They made percussion instruments from materials found around them, including hollow gourds and wood. Rattles and scrapers are among their most recognizable musical legacies. The sounds of modern maracas and the güiro still help shape salsa’s rhythm.

European diseases, forced labor and violence devastated Taíno communities. This loss, along with the limited surviving records, makes it difficult to trace their exact musical influence on salsa. We can’t reconstruct Taíno dances from the evidence we have, but neither did their culture disappear. Indigenous ancestry, traditions, words and knowledge remain part of the Caribbean today.

Sources

  • Salsa Dance: Complete Overview & Guide - Salsa Vida
  • Arte del mar: Artistic Exchange in the Caribbean - The Metropolitan Museum of Art
  • Música Jíbara: Aguinaldos and Fiesta de Reyes - Smithsonian Folkways
  • Indigenous Legacy of the Caribbean Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibition - Smithsonian Institution
  • Columbus and the Taíno - Library of Congress

The Taíno people

The Taíno are Indigenous to the Caribbean. More than 2,000 years ago, some of their ancestors traveled by canoe from northern South America to the islands, bringing Arawakan languages and crops such as cassava. In Cuba and the neighboring islands, families grated cassava roots and baked the flour into thin rounds of bread called casabe.

At gatherings called areítos, people sang and danced together to pass on memories of their ancestors. Today, Taíno descendants across the Caribbean still make casabe and keep family stories alive.

Sources
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • Taíno: Native Heritage and Identity in the Caribbean - National Museum of the American Indian
  • Taino Settlement - National Park Service

The bohío

A bohío is a traditional dwelling built from materials such as wood and palm thatch. Taíno communities farmed, fished, traded and gathered in shared spaces. Their homes and gathering places remind us that the Caribbean already had complex societies, with everyday music and dance as well as ceremonial traditions, before European arrival.

Sources
  • Taino Settlement - National Park Service

The güiro

Run a stick over the grooves of a güiro and you get a distinctive rasp. A long scrape followed by short strokes can create a repeating rhythmic pattern. Modern salsa musicians use the güiro to add texture to the percussion section. The name güiro comes from a Taíno word for the fruit of the higüero, or calabash tree. Its hard shell can be hollowed out and carved with grooves to make the instrument.

Sources
  • Salsa Instruments: A Complete Guide with Audio Examples - Salsa Vida
  • From These Lands Visual Description Tour - Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
  • Güiro - National Museum of American History
  • Música Jíbara: Aguinaldos and Fiesta de Reyes - Smithsonian Folkways

The maracas

Maracas are hollow rattles filled with seeds or other small pieces. Shaken in pairs, they can produce surprisingly precise rhythms. Indigenous Caribbean peoples used rattles before colonization, and maracas later became part of Cuban son and Puerto Rican ensembles. Listen for their crisp sound weaving between the louder drums in a salsa recording.

Sources
  • Salsa Instruments: A Complete Guide with Audio Examples - Salsa Vida

CHAPTER 03 / 16 · LANGUAGE, MUSIC AND PARTNER DANCE

What Spain Brought to Cuba

Spain and Cuba · The colonial centuries

Most salsa songs are sung in Spanish. The language came to Cuba with Spanish colonists and became the island’s main language over centuries of colonial rule. Settlers also brought guitars, staff notation and partner dances that Cuban musicians and dancers adapted over generations.

Spanish took root in Cuba through centuries of colonial rule and became its principal language. The Spanish spoken on the island also absorbed words from the people who already lived there. The güiro on the previous page carries a Taíno name into Spanish and into the vocabulary of salsa musicians today.

Spanish settlers brought songs accompanied by guitar and a way of writing music on a five-line staff. A guitarist could strum beneath a singer or pick out a tune between verses. Cuban players developed the tres, whose paired strings gave son its ringing sound. The piano arrived later. Cuban composer Ignacio Cervantes drew on the island’s dance rhythms in his short piano pieces, and the piano later became a mainstay of salsa bands.

European social dances also spread through the Caribbean. Contradanza, a dance performed by multiple couples, eventually developed Cuban forms in which pairs had more freedom to dance together. The influence came from several parts of Europe as well as Spain, and the music and steps changed as they circulated through the islands.

Cuba’s musicians didn’t simply reproduce European traditions. They combined Spanish-language singing and harmonic structures with rhythms and musical practices shaped by African and Indigenous Caribbean communities. This combination of melody, harmony and rhythm would become central to son and, eventually, salsa.

The dancing couple

Spanish settlers brought European ballroom customs to Cuba. At a Havana ball in 1803, dancers opened with a court minuet, then joined other couples for the turning figures of a contradanza. In the Cuban danzón that followed in the nineteenth century, each pair could turn and travel independently. Salsa partners still share that freedom to improvise together.

Sources

  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida

  • The Origin and Development of Cuban Popular Music Genres and Their Incorporation into Academic Compositions - University of Georgia

The courtyard

The décima, a Spanish verse form with ten rhyming lines, found a home in rural Cuba. At a gathering, one singer might improvise a décima to the sound of plucked strings and another reply in rhyme. Early son singers drew on that tradition. In salsa, a lead singer called a sonero still invents verses between repeats of the chorus.

Sources
  • An Introduction to the Son - Smithsonian Folkways
  • Punto - UNESCO

The stringed instrument

Spanish settlers brought guitars to Cuba and used them to accompany songs. A player could strum chords beneath a verse, then pick out a tune between lines. Cuban musicians developed the tres from this guitar tradition. Its paired strings gave son a distinctive sound, and salsa pianists later adapted its repeating patterns for the keyboard.

Sources
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • An Introduction to the Son - Smithsonian Folkways

The Spanish reading primer

A cartilla was a small book that taught children to read, starting with letters and syllables. Under Spanish colonial rule, Spanish became the main language across much of the Caribbean, including Cuba and Puerto Rico. Many musicians who shaped salsa in New York came from those islands, among them Cuba’s Celia Cruz and Puerto Rico’s Héctor Lavoe. Today, most salsa songs are still sung in Spanish.

Sources

The sheet music

Spanish settlers brought guitars, folk songs and European traditions of melody and harmony to Cuba. Chord progressions gave songs a sense of movement, tension and resolution. Written notation let composers create and share arrangements for entire orchestras.

Cuban musicians blended these traditions with Taíno percussion and African rhythms. In son cubano, Spanish-influenced melodies and guitar chords intertwine with the rhythms of clave and bongó. In danzón, flute and violins carry elegant melodies over timbales and güiro.

You can still hear that fusion in a salsa piano montuno. The pianist turns a European-style chord progression into a syncopated pattern, making harmony itself part of the groove.

CHAPTER 04 / 16 · AFRICAN MUSIC, MOVEMENT AND FAITH

Africa: The Rhythmic and Spiritual Roots

West and Central Africa and Cuba · 1500s–1800s

Enslaved Africans brought diverse traditions of drumming, dance, call-and-response singing and spiritual practice to Cuba. Despite slavery and repression, they preserved and reimagined those traditions. Their influence is at the heart of salsa’s rhythm, expressive body movement and Afro-Cuban dance vocabulary.

Over several centuries, the Atlantic slave trade forced people from many parts of Africa to Cuba. Among them were people from the Kongo region of Central Africa and Yoruba-speaking communities in West Africa. Each community brought its own songs, dances and religious traditions.

In many of these traditions, several drums play different but complementary patterns. A singer’s call can be answered by a chorus, and dancers respond to the rhythm through grounded steps, bent knees and expressive body movements. These ideas took on new forms in Cuban music and dance.

Religion was another important source of creativity and cultural survival. In Cuba, Yoruba-derived Lucumí religious traditions developed alongside other African-derived faiths, including Kongo-derived Palo. Songs and movements associated with orishas, or divine beings, have their own ceremonial meanings. Some have also entered folkloric performances and the movement vocabulary of salsa dancers. Sacred dances remain living practices in their own right.

Sources

The dancers

In many African-derived dance traditions, the torso, shoulders and hips are active participants in the rhythm. Cuban rumba and other Afro-Cuban forms developed distinct ways of expressing that relationship between movement and music. Salsa dancers today often draw on those forms during solo footwork, body movement and musical breaks.

Sources
  • Cuban Dance Styles: The Complete List - Salsa Vida
  • A Musical Revelation: Kongo Music Past and Present - The Metropolitan Museum of Art
  • Salsa and Migration - National Park Service

The drums

The hand drummers in this Kongo-inspired gathering each have a part to play. One can hold a repeating pattern while another varies the accents. In Cuba, musicians of Central African descent passed down distinct drumming and dance traditions, including yuka and makuta.

Bàtá drums belong to a different history. Yoruba-speaking peoples of West Africa brought musical and religious traditions to Cuba, where Lucumí musicians developed ensembles of three double-headed bàtá drums. The players answer one another and accompany songs and dances for the orishas. Each orisha has its own rhythms and movements.

Sources
  • Cuban Dance Styles: The Complete List - Salsa Vida
  • Cuban Dance Styles: The Complete List - Salsa Vida

  • Havana, Cuba, ca. 1957: Rhythms and Songs for the Orishas - Smithsonian Folkways
  • Bàtá (ìyáàlù) drum - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

The answering voices

One singer calls, the chorus answers. Because the chorus knows its refrain, the lead singer is free to improvise new words and rhythms. This call-and-response structure is central to many African and Afro-Cuban musical traditions. In salsa, the repeating chorus is called the coro, and the lead singer can improvise soneos in between.

CHAPTER 05 / 16 · THE AFRO-CUBAN FUSION

Cuban Son: The Sound That Became Salsa

Oriente and Havana, Cuba · Late 1800s–1930s

In Cuba, musicians fused European song and strings with African-derived percussion and singing, alongside Indigenous Caribbean instruments. Son cubano emerged as one of the clearest expressions of this blend. Its rhythms, melodies and partner dancing became a direct foundation of salsa.

In Cuba, Africans and their descendants formed mutual-aid societies called cabildos. These gatherings helped Cubans of Yoruba descent pass down the songs, dances and batá drum rhythms they used to honor their deities, the orishas.

In parts of mainland North America, colonial laws barred enslaved people from playing drums. In Cuba, generations of musicians kept African drumming traditions alive, giving drums a more prominent role in the island’s music.

Son took shape in eastern Cuba around the turn of the twentieth century. Musicians combined Spanish-language songs and string accompaniment with African-derived rhythms and call-and-response singing. Claves, bongos, maracas and the tres helped define its sound. The dancers, meanwhile, developed their own ways of moving together to the music.

Son spread to Havana, where groups such as the Sexteto Habanero popularized it. Trumpets joined the ensemble, and later bands such as Arsenio Rodríguez’s expanded the sound with piano and congas. Radio, records and touring musicians carried son abroad. Many of the ingredients of modern salsa were now in place.

The son dancers

Son was both a musical genre and a partner dance. Couples learned to shift their weight together, often using contratiempo timing that emphasizes the space around the music’s main accents. Son’s close partnership, turns and rhythmic expression helped shape later Cuban dances and the mambo tradition. Son is still danced in Cuba and beyond today.

Sources
  • Son Cubano - Salsa Vida
  • The practice of Cuban Son - UNESCO

The Cuban tres

The Cuban tres has three pairs of strings. A tresero often plays a guajeo, a short, syncopated pattern that repeats against the bass and percussion while the singer moves freely above it. In this rendition of “Guantanamera,” listen for the bright, doubled sound as the player picks out the tune. Salsa pianists later took up the tresero’s role, weaving repeating patterns through the rhythm section.

“Guantanamera” on the Cuban tres · Watch on YouTube

The Oriente sign

Oriente was the historic province in eastern Cuba associated with early son. Musicians carried the sound from rural gatherings to the city of Santiago de Cuba and eventually Havana. The migration of musicians and the spread of records helped turn a regional tradition into one of Cuba’s most important musical exports.

CHAPTER 06 / 16 · A DANCE REVOLUTION

Cuba’s Golden Age of Music and Dance

Cuba · Late 1800s–early 1960s

Cuba produced an astonishing variety of dances: rumba, danzón, mambo, cha-cha-cha, pachanga and casino, as well as son. Each had its own sound and movement. Cuban bands found eager audiences across Latin America and the United States.

By the early twentieth century, Cuban music was evolving in several directions at once. Afro-Cuban rumba flourished in communities around Havana and Matanzas. Danzón, rooted in earlier Cuban and European social dances, became a celebrated partner dance. Son spread across the island and into the recording industry.

In the late 1930s, Cuban musicians began transforming the danzón with new rhythms and repeated, energetic passages. Mambo emerged from this experimentation. In the 1950s, Enrique Jorrín popularized cha-cha-cha, and by the end of the decade, pachanga was the latest craze. Cuban dancers were also creating casino and its group form, rueda de casino, drawing on earlier dances while developing their own turns and partner patterns.

Records, films and touring bands carried Cuban music to Mexico, Puerto Rico, New York and beyond. In New York, dancers packed the Palladium Ballroom for mambo.

The rumba gathering

Cuban rumba grew primarily from Afro-Cuban communities. Percussion, singing, handclaps and expressive movement are central to it. Guaguancó, one form of rumba, includes a playful exchange between dancers. Rumba remains its own living tradition, but its rhythmic and movement vocabulary has also become an important influence on salsa.

Sources
  • Cuban Dance Styles - Salsa Vida
  • Rumba in Cuba - UNESCO

The charanga orchestra

Danzón emerged in nineteenth-century Cuba from earlier social dance music. A traditional charanga ensemble features flute, violins, bass, timbales and güiro; later lineups added other instruments. Its elegant sound evolved into new forms, including the danzón-mambo and cha-cha-cha. Listen for the contrast between a charanga’s strings and the brass-heavy salsa bands that would follow.

Sources
  • Latin Jazz Glossary - Smithsonian National Museum of American History
  • Mambo - Oxford Bibliographies

The mambo record

Cuban brothers Orestes and Israel “Cachao” López helped develop the rhythmic ideas behind mambo. Bandleader Dámaso Pérez Prado later brought a big-band version to Mexico, where his recordings became international hits. Mambo’s syncopated music encouraged inventive partnerwork, turns and solo steps, laying an important foundation for modern salsa dance.

Sources
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • Mambo - Oxford Bibliographies

The cha-cha-cha couple

Cha-cha-cha took shape in Havana’s dance halls in the early 1950s. In a Cuban charanga orchestra, flute and violins carry the melody over the steady scrape of the güiro. Partners rock forward or back, return their weight to the other foot, then take three small steps to the side. The name cha-cha-cha echoes the shuffle of their shoes.

Violinist Enrique Jorrín wrote “La engañadora” with dancers in mind and recorded it with Orquesta América. Try counting “two, three, cha-cha-cha” along with the recording. The last three syllables fit the little shuffle.

“La engañadora” by Enrique Jorrín · Watch on YouTube

Sources
  • Cha Cha Cha - Salsa Vida
  • Cuban Dance Styles: The Complete List - Salsa Vida
  • Cha-Cha-Chá - Cubans in America

The pachanga dancer

Watch the knees. A bend and release gives pachanga its bounce, even when the feet slide or twist along the floor. Cuban composer Eduardo Davidson wrote “La Pachanga” in 1959. Within two years New Yorkers were dancing it at the Palladium. Salsa dancers still borrow its footwork for shines, the solo steps they dance when partners let go.

Sources
  • Pachanga - Salsa Vida
  • Pachanga (1961), John A. Lucchese - Library of Dance
  • The Jukebox: Cuba’s Revenge (1961) - Time

The rueda de casino

Cuban casino developed its own circular partner movement. In rueda de casino, several couples form a circle and a caller announces moves that everyone performs together, often changing partners. This Cuban tradition continued to evolve and became one of the most recognizable forms of salsa dancing around the world.

Sources

CHAPTER 07 / 16 · THE GOLDEN AGE OF MAMBO

The Palladium: New York’s Mambo Era

Midtown Manhattan, New York · 1947–1966

In the 1950s, mambo took the United States by storm, and New York’s Palladium Ballroom was its epicenter. The era’s greatest Latin bands and dancers shared one floor, creating an exciting new style of partner dancing that would become the foundation of modern salsa.

New York became a meeting place for Cuban, Puerto Rican and other musicians. At Broadway and 53rd Street, the Palladium offered live Latin music four nights a week. The three kings of the ballroom, Machito, Tito Puente and Tito Rodríguez, drove dancers to new heights with their orchestras, often sharing the bill and competing to win over the crowd.

The Palladium brought people together across racial and cultural lines. Latino, Black, Italian, Irish, Jewish and other New Yorkers danced to the same bands. Mambo dancers combined Cuban son and rumba with influences from swing, jazz, tap and other dance traditions. The result was an increasingly inventive style, full of turns, shines, showmanship and musical improvisation.

Wednesday nights featured a lesson by “Killer Joe” Piro, amateur competitions and professional shows. Stars such as Cuban Pete and Millie Donay, Augie and Margo, and the Mambo Aces helped raise the standard of the dance. When the Palladium closed in 1966, the mambo craze was fading, but its music and movement lived on in the salsa scene taking shape in New York.

Sources

  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • Palladium Ballroom - Palladium Mambo

The mambo dancers

Some of the Palladium’s most influential dancers were Cuban Pete and Millie Donay, Augie and Margo, and the Mambo Aces, Aníbal “Andy” Vázquez and Joe Centeno. They combined partnerwork with intricate solo steps, later called shines, and brought their own flavor to the dance. The Mambo Aces took their act to television in 1957.

Live music

Dancers at the Palladium might hear two orchestras in a single night. Machito, Tito Puente and Tito Rodríguez each led one of the ballroom’s “Big Three” bands. From the floor you could hear the brass section punch out a phrase and a timbalero answer it with a roll. Drummer and bandleader Puente played for the Wednesday mambo contests, too. A 1956 photograph shows his band playing while the judges watch the dancers.

Frank “Killer Joe” Piro

On Wednesdays, Frank “Killer Joe” Piro taught a dance lesson from nine to ten, then took the microphone to host the amateur contest and the professional show. A newcomer could spend an hour learning from Piro and stay to see what experienced dancers did with the same floor.

CHAPTER 08 / 16 · A NEW SOUND FOR LATIN AMERICA

Fania Records and the Birth of Salsa

New York City · 1964–early 1970s

In 1964, Johnny Pacheco and Jerry Masucci founded Fania Records. The label united some of New York’s most exciting Latin musicians and helped popularize the name “salsa.” A new generation of artists transformed Caribbean musical traditions into a powerful sound that spoke to Latinos around the world.

Even as the mambo era was ending, the Latin music scene in New York was alive with experimentation. Cuban son and other Caribbean genres mingled with jazz, soul and the sounds of the city. Puerto Rican communities were central to this new scene, as were musicians with roots across the Caribbean.

Fania Records began in 1964, founded by Dominican bandleader Johnny Pacheco and lawyer Jerry Masucci. They built a roster of extraordinary talent, including Willie Colón, Héctor Lavoe and Ray Barretto, and assembled the Fania All-Stars, a supergroup of musicians who normally led or performed in their own bands.

The Spanish word salsa means sauce, a fitting name for this blend of musical ingredients. Fania didn’t invent all the music or necessarily coin the word, but its recordings, films and promotion helped turn salsa into an internationally recognized genre. The All-Stars’ 1971 concert at New York’s Cheetah club and the film Our Latin Thing (1972) captured the excitement of a new musical movement rooted in Latino life in the city.

Sources
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • Salsa Dance: Complete Overview & Guide - Salsa Vida
  • Fania History Timeline - Fania Records
  • Salsa Is More Than Salsa - National Park Service
  • Fania All Stars Live in Japan 1976 - Fania Records

Johnny Pacheco and Jerry Masucci

Pacheco was an experienced bandleader born in the Dominican Republic. Masucci brought legal and business experience. Together they launched Fania in 1964, giving musicians a platform to record and reach new audiences. Pacheco later led the Fania All-Stars as musical director, while Masucci promoted the label internationally.

The salsa records

Before salsa became the common name, listeners often identified the music by genres such as son, mambo or guaracha. The salsa label helped connect these sounds with the newer music coming out of New York. Record covers, radio, DJs and promoters such as Izzy Sanabria helped give the scene a recognizable identity.

The Fania All-Stars

What happens when you bring the leaders and stars of several bands together? Fania did exactly that in 1968 at New York’s Red Garter club. The ensemble grew into a showcase for the label’s top singers and instrumentalists. Its live concerts became a celebration of individual musicianship and a shared Latin musical identity.

Over the years, the lineup featured singers such as Celia Cruz, Héctor Lavoe, Cheo Feliciano and Ismael Miranda alongside bandleaders Johnny Pacheco, Willie Colón, Ray Barretto and Bobby Valentín.

The Fania All-Stars’ 1971 show at the Cheetah club was recorded and filmed. The resulting documentary, Our Latin Thing (Nuestra Cosa Latina), came out in 1972. It connected the musicians onstage with scenes of Latino life in New York, giving audiences outside the city a window into the community that shaped salsa.

CHAPTER 09 / 16 · THE FANIA ALL-STARS AT YANKEE STADIUM

Salsa Takes the World Stage

The Bronx, New York · August 1973

In 1973, tens of thousands of fans packed Yankee Stadium to see the Fania All-Stars. Salsa had grown from the dance halls of New York into a cultural movement. Concerts, films and recordings soon carried that music across Latin America, Europe, Africa and Asia.

The Fania All-Stars’ concert at Yankee Stadium in August 1973 was a milestone for Latin music. The lineup brought together stars such as Johnny Pacheco, Héctor Lavoe, Willie Colón and Ray Barretto, with Cuban percussionist Mongo Santamaría joining as a guest. Salsa had reached one of America’s most famous stadiums.

When Barretto and Santamaría traded conga solos, excited fans rushed onto the field and the concert ended early. Yet the event demonstrated just how much the music meant to its audience. Footage from the stadium and a later Puerto Rico concert was combined in the 1976 film Salsa, preserving the energy of the movement for viewers elsewhere.

Fania’s reach went well beyond New York. The All-Stars toured Latin America, performed in Kinshasa, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), in 1974, and reached Japan and Europe in 1976. Salsa was becoming an international language of music and dance, with a life far beyond the city where it had taken its name.

Johnny Pacheco

The co-founder of Fania Records served as the musical director of the All-Stars. With so many stars sharing one stage, the band needed someone to bring the musicians together. Pacheco’s conducting and his background as a flautist, percussionist and bandleader helped shape the ensemble’s sound.

Héctor Lavoe

Born in Ponce, Puerto Rico, Lavoe became one of the most distinctive voices of New York salsa. His recordings with Willie Colón made him a star, and he later built a major solo career. Known as El Cantante de los Cantantes, he combined an unmistakable voice with the ability to improvise over a repeating chorus.

Willie Colón

A New York-born musician of Puerto Rican heritage, Colón helped define a gritty, urban salsa sound. His trombone-driven band and partnership with Lavoe produced influential records, starting with El Malo in 1967. He later collaborated with artists such as Rubén Blades, showing how salsa could tell stories about life, identity and society.

Ray Barretto

The New York-born percussionist brought experience in both jazz and Latin music to the All-Stars. A skilled conguero and bandleader, he could create a conversation across his drums with open tones, slaps and quick rhythmic phrases. His “Congo Bongo” exchange with Mongo Santamaría is one of the most memorable moments associated with the stadium show.

Born in Havana, Mongo Santamaría helped bring Afro-Cuban percussion to international audiences through Latin music and jazz. At Yankee Stadium, he faced Ray Barretto in a conga exchange. Their musical conversation linked two generations and traditions of Cuban and New York Latin music, with the crowd responding to every burst of energy.

A stadium concert gave salsa a scale previously associated with major pop and rock acts. Fania later released Live at Yankee Stadium, a collection that also includes recordings made in Puerto Rico. CHAPTER 10 / 16 · FORMALIZING SALSA DANCE

Eddie Torres and the Rise of New York On2

New York City · 1970s–1990s

Eddie Torres helped turn New York’s mambo and salsa traditions into a method that dancers everywhere could learn. With guidance from June LaBerta and performances alongside his wife Maria and Tito Puente, he popularized On2 timing, trained influential dancers and helped elevate salsa as a performance art.

Eddie Torres grew up studying the mambo dancers he saw in New York clubs. When he began teaching, he worked with ballroom mambo instructor June LaBerta to put names and musical counts to his steps. His teaching method gave students a consistent way to learn and communicate movements that had often been passed down informally.

The Eddie Torres On2 basic steps on counts 1, 2, 3 and 5, 6, 7, with the main direction changes on 2 and 6. This became one of the most widely taught approaches to New York-style salsa. His instructional VHS tapes allowed dancers far from New York to study the method, practice shines and learn partnerwork.

Eddie and his wife and dance partner Maria began performing with Tito Puente’s orchestra in 1980. His dance company, the Eddie Torres Dancers, helped bring mambo to larger stages. Students including Adolfo Indacochea went on to teach and perform internationally. Torres didn’t invent dancing On2, but he played a major role in making it accessible to generations of dancers.

Sources
  • Eddie Torres - Salsa Vida
  • New York Style Salsa (Salsa On 2) - Salsa Vida
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida
  • About Eddie Torres - Eddie and Maria Torres
  • Mambo On 2: The Birth of a New Form of Dance in New York City - Centro Journal

Eddie Torres

Eddie is known as the Mambo King for his work as a performer, choreographer and teacher. His partnership with Maria Torres and performances with Tito Puente helped keep the dance tradition visible. His collaboration with June LaBerta made it easier to teach, and his company helped launch generations of performers and instructors.

Eddie Torres teaches the On2 basic · Watch on YouTube

  • Mambo On 2: The Birth of a New Form of Dance in New York City - Centro Journal

The On2 count

On2 does not mean that a dancer necessarily takes the first step on beat two. In Eddie’s method, dancers step on 1, 2, 3 and 5, 6, 7. The break steps, where the basic changes direction, occur on 2 and 6. This is a key distinction between the Eddie Torres style and the On1 method you’ll meet on the next page.

Sources
  • New York Style Salsa (Salsa On 2) - Salsa Vida
  • Mambo On 2: The Birth of a New Form of Dance in New York City - Centro Journal

The Slot

New York salsa dancers call the narrow lane they share the slot. In a cross-body lead, the leader steps aside, the follower travels straight through, and the partners turn to face each other from opposite ends. They can trade places again or break away for shines before meeting back in the slot.

Sources
  • New York Style Salsa (Salsa On 2) - Salsa Vida

The instructional VHS tape

Before YouTube and online classes, an instructional videotape could bring a New York salsa teacher into your living room. Eddie Torres’s VHS lessons helped popularize his footwork, timing and terminology beyond his local classes. Dancers could rewind a difficult step, practice it repeatedly and share what they learned at their own studios.

Sources
  • Eddie Torres - Salsa Vida
  • History of Salsa Dance - Salsa Vida

CHAPTER 11 / 16 · WEST COAST ON1

LA Style: Salsa Gets a Hollywood Flair

Los Angeles, California · 1990s onward

On the West Coast, dancers developed a flashy approach to salsa built around On1 timing, rapid turns and dramatic showmanship. The Vázquez brothers and other Los Angeles dancers helped popularize LA style, which became one of the most widely taught styles of salsa around the world.

Los Angeles had a Latin music and dance scene of its own, shaped by its Mexican, Central American and other communities. By the 1990s, Francisco, Luis and Johnny Vázquez were among the dancers helping develop and popularize a distinctive West Coast approach to salsa.

Like New York style, LA salsa is generally danced in a line, but its break steps fall on counts 1 and 5 rather than 2 and 6. The style became associated with sharp turns, energetic shines and dramatic partnerwork. Performance teams such as Los Rumberos and Salsa Brava brought that energy to stages, where routines could include dips, lifts and acrobatics.

The showy style fit naturally into the world of entertainment and dance competitions, while On1 timing gave many new dancers an accessible way to start. Workshops, touring performers and the growing congress circuit helped carry it far beyond California. Other salsa scenes were developing their own approaches too, including one with an especially strong identity in Colombia.

Johnny Vázquez

Johnny and his brothers Francisco and Luis are often credited as leading figures in LA-style salsa. Francisco founded Los Rumberos, Luis co-founded Salsa Brava, and Johnny later founded Imperio Azteka. Their stage routines, teaching and international appearances helped make LA salsa recognizable around the world.

Johnny Vázquez and Olivia Dasso in Milan, 1999 · Watch on YouTube

The On1 count

Both the LA On1 and Eddie Torres On2 basics usually have six weight changes in an eight-count. In On1, the main direction changes are on counts 1 and 5. In On2, they are on 2 and 6. Try counting along to a song and notice how the same music can support different ways of dancing.

  • New York Style Salsa (Salsa On 2) - Salsa Vida

The stage lights

On a theater stage, dancers can use bigger movements, multiple spins and dramatic finishes to reach an audience. LA teams became known for this kind of showmanship. The social version of LA salsa, however, doesn’t require acrobatics: the same timing, turns and partnerwork can fit comfortably on a crowded dance floor.

CHAPTER 12 / 16 · SALSA CALEÑA

Cali: Colombia’s Capital of Salsa

Cali, Colombia · 1960s–present

As salsa traveled across Latin America, Cali developed a musical and dance culture of its own. Influenced by Caribbean records and Colombian traditions, salsa caleña became famous for its lightning-fast footwork. The city’s clubs, dance schools and performers helped make Cali a world capital of salsa.

While salsa was taking shape in New York, people in Cali were already listening and dancing to Cuban and other Caribbean music. Records arrived through the port of Buenaventura, and radio, cinema and local dance halls helped the music reach new audiences. Colombian cumbia and porro were among the traditions that shaped the city’s dancers.

In the 1960s and 1970s, mambo, pachanga, boogaloo and salsa became part of Cali’s nightlife. Local DJs sometimes played records at faster speeds, encouraging dancers to invent quick steps, kicks and flicks. The style grew into salsa caleña, with its own rhythmic footwork, lively partner movement and a strong sense of local identity.

Cali’s dance schools train children, social dancers and professional teams. Companies such as Swing Latino earned an international following with their fast, synchronized footwork and acrobatics. At home, dancers have a year-round audience, from full-length shows like Delirio to the crowds who line the streets for the Feria de Cali each December.

Sources
  • Salsa Dance: Complete Overview & Guide - Salsa Vida
  • La Vieja Guardia: Salsa Dancing in Cali, Colombia - Smithsonian Folklife

  • La salsa caleña… única en el mundo - City of Cali
  • Salsa in Cali - Colombia Travel

The speeding record player

Cali’s dancers became famous for keeping up with records played at faster speeds. Local accounts describe DJs speeding up boogaloo records from 33 to 45 rpm in the 1960s, creating a sound that inspired new footwork. It’s one part of a wider story of musicians, record collectors and dancers adapting imported music to local tastes.

Sources
  • La Vieja Guardia: Salsa Dancing in Cali, Colombia - Smithsonian Folklife
  • La salsa caleña… única en el mundo - City of Cali

The caleña dancers

Salsa caleña is known for intricate kicks, taps, quick changes of weight and expressive footwork. Partners often dance around one another rather than staying in the narrow slot associated with LA and New York styles. The fast steps are characteristic of the dance, but traditional social dancing and elaborate stage choreography are not the same thing.

Sources
  • Salsa Dance: Complete Overview & Guide - Salsa Vida
  • La Vieja Guardia: Salsa Dancing in Cali, Colombia - Smithsonian Folklife

Performances and shows

In Cali, a salsa performance can fill a whole evening. Delirio brings caleña dancers, circus artists and a live orchestra together under one tent. Each December the city takes its choreography into the streets for the Feria de Cali. In the Salsódromo parade, dance schools perform one after another for crowds lining the route.

Competitive salsa

Competition runs deep in Cali’s dance schools. Young dancers enter local qualifiers, rehearsing in pairs or teams for a chance to represent their school at the Festival Mundial de Salsa. For its 2025 competition, the city announced a field of 1,300 artists across the amateur, professional and elite divisions. Cali’s teams have also made their mark abroad. At the 2007 World Salsa Championships near Orlando, teams from the city swept the medals in the team event.

CHAPTER 13 / 16 · THE FIRST SALSA CONGRESS

Puerto Rico Hosts the First World Salsa Congress

San Juan, Puerto Rico · 1997

In 1997, Elí Irizarry brought salsa dancers from around the world together in Puerto Rico for the first World Salsa Congress. For many, it was a chance to experience other styles in person. The gathering launched a festival format that would transform the way salsa dancers learned, traveled and connected.

Before YouTube, salsa dancers often learned the styles and techniques common in their own cities. An On2 dancer from New York, an On1 dancer from Los Angeles and a casino dancer from Cuba might all love the same music but have very different ways of moving to it.

In 1997, Puerto Rican producer Elí Irizarry organized the first World Salsa Congress in San Juan. He dedicated the event to Palladium-era dancer Aníbal Vázquez of the Mambo Aces. International participants came to learn, perform and dance together, and the program included discussions of the history of salsa music and dance.

Workshops, rehearsed shows and nights of social dancing became familiar parts of the congress weekend. Competition came later in Puerto Rico. In 2002 the congress hosted the first World Salsa Open, giving dancers another reason to travel to San Juan.

Workshops

At the first congress in San Juan, visiting dancers could learn directly from teachers whose steps they had only seen onstage or heard about back home. Elí Irizarry also set aside time for the history of the music and dance. Workshops became a daytime fixture at salsa festivals, where dancers still travel to study a particular style or teacher.

  • Salsa Congress - Salsa Vida
  • Reunidos por la salsa - La Nación

Social dancing

In 1997, dancers from around the world met on the social floor in San Juan. For many, it was their first chance to dance with a partner who had learned a different timing or a different way to lead a turn. Changing partners let them try those differences for themselves. Late-night socials are still where dancers from different scenes meet at festivals around the world.

Performances

Puerto Rico’s congress gave visiting companies a stage and an audience of fellow dancers. By its second edition in 1998, 32 salsa companies were taking part in shows and workshops. The evening showcase became a congress tradition. A team can rehearse a routine at home, then take it abroad and perform for dancers who have never seen its local style.

  • Reunidos por la salsa - La Nación

Competitions

The first Puerto Rico World Salsa Congress took place in 1997. In 2002 it hosted the first World Salsa Open, drawing couples to San Juan to compete for an international title. Many festivals now set aside part of the weekend for competition, with separate divisions for different styles or experience levels.

CHAPTER 14 / 16 · THE WORLDWIDE CONGRESS CIRCUIT

Salsa Becomes a Global Dance Community

Worldwide · 1999 onward

Salsa congresses spread from Puerto Rico to Los Angeles, Europe, Asia and beyond. International instructors and dance teams began traveling from city to city, sharing steps and styles. The Internet accelerated that exchange, connecting local dance communities into a worldwide salsa scene.

Promoter Albert Torres organized the West Coast Salsa Congress in Los Angeles in 1999, helping expand the congress movement. By the early 2000s, events in Japan and Europe were welcoming visiting instructors, performers and dancers. The 2000 Japan Salsa Congress even held auditions for local teams to perform at the following year’s event in Los Angeles.

As the circuit grew, dancers learned more than the styles they grew up with. On1 and On2 dancers incorporated Afro-Cuban body movement, Colombian performers experimented with new partnerwork, and instructors developed ways of teaching to international audiences. Local dance cultures continued to evolve even as a more widely shared vocabulary took shape.

Online videos and social media made this exchange faster than ever. Dancers could study performances from around the world, discover teachers and plan trips around festivals. Today, there are salsa congresses and festivals across continents. You can travel thousands of miles, walk into a room full of strangers and still find someone to dance with.

The traveling dancers

As the festival calendar filled out, salsa dancers began planning trips around the social dancing as well as the classes. In Europe, dancers could spend one weekend in Berlin, another in Milan, and find familiar partners on both floors. These trips linked local scenes across borders. Even when partners spoke different languages, they could still share a song.

CHAPTER 15 / 16 · WORLD SALSA CHAMPIONSHIPS ON ESPN

Salsa Becomes a World-Class Competitive Sport

Lake Buena Vista, Florida · December 2007

Beginning in 2005, the World Salsa Championships put competitive salsa on an international stage and on ESPN. Elite dancers from around the world pushed the limits of technique, musicality and athleticism, helping establish salsa as a serious competitive discipline and paving the way for more international championships.

Salsa competitions had been part of the dance scene since the Palladium era, but the World Salsa Championships, launched in Las Vegas in 2005, brought a new level of international visibility. The event featured separate divisions for different styles, including On1, On2, cabaret and teams, allowing dancers to compete against others in their own discipline.

In 2007, the third edition took place at Disney’s Coronado Springs Resort near Orlando, with organizers announcing dancers from more than 40 countries. ESPN carried the competition to audiences beyond the salsa community. Australians Oliver Pineda and Luda Kroitor won the On2 division for the third consecutive year, while teams from Cali took all three top places in the team event.

These championships helped set a benchmark for competitive salsa. Later events such as the World Latin Dance Cup and Euroson Latino continued raising the level of the art form. Competitive dancers now train for speed, strength, precision and musical expression, turning competitive salsa into a demanding athletic discipline, in addition to being a popular social dance.

The competing couple

Championship divisions put different skills on display. In On1 and On2, partners must show control, timing and musicality in their chosen style. In cabaret, lifts and acrobatic elements add another level of difficulty. The Australian team of Oliver Pineda and Luda Kroitor became a standout example of On2 excellence at these early championships.

The judging panel

At this level, even small details matter. Judges evaluate how dancers interpret the music, execute choreography and work together. A difficult spin means little if the couple loses its balance or timing afterward. Separate divisions and published criteria help make competitive salsa more structured while leaving room for creativity.

Couples and teams represented their countries, judges scored their routines, and a world title was at stake. For dancers who spent months training for a few minutes onstage, a place on a sports network brought recognition for that work and an audience well beyond the salsa clubs.

CHAPTER 16 / 16 · A NEW GENERATION TAKES THE FLOOR

Salsa at the Super Bowl

Santa Clara, California · February 8, 2026

In 2026, Bad Bunny put salsa in the spotlight at the Super Bowl LX halftime show. Alongside Lady Gaga, a live salsa band and professional dancers, he brought a centuries-old Caribbean legacy to one of the world’s biggest entertainment stages, inspiring a new generation to discover the dance.

Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl LX halftime show was a celebration of Puerto Rican culture, community and unity. A sequence of scenes brought viewers from the island’s sugarcane fields and neighborhood gatherings to a wedding reception, where a salsa band took center stage. Lady Gaga sang a salsa arrangement of “Die With a Smile” and danced with Bad Bunny.

The show then moved into “Baile Inolvidable,” his 2025 salsa hit, with professional salsa dancers from Puerto Rico, Los Angeles and beyond. For the salsa community, this was a landmark moment: the dance was a featured part of the show, performed by artists who had devoted years to their craft, not simply background choreography.

The music that grew from Cuba’s cultural encounters, took shape under the name salsa in New York, and traveled across generations and continents had reached another extraordinary stage. But the story doesn’t end with a stadium or a television broadcast. It continues in every dance class, every club and every person discovering the joy of salsa for the first time. The next chapter is yours to dance.

Bad Bunny and Lady Gaga

Bad Bunny’s 2025 song “Baile Inolvidable” brought renewed attention to salsa among younger listeners. The wedding band

The Puerto Rican band Los Sobrinos accompanied Lady Gaga’s salsa performance during the wedding scene. The wedding itself was real. The show then featured “Baile Inolvidable,” with dancers including Tito Ortos and Tamara Livolsi and performers connected to the Los Angeles scene. It brought together the music and the dance as a celebration of Puerto Rican life.

La Casita

La Casita, the pink house, evoked a Puerto Rican home where friends and family gather to celebrate. Guests including Karol G, Cardi B and Pedro Pascal danced and watched from the porch. The image was a reminder of what makes salsa special: it belongs not just on grand stages, but in homes, neighborhoods and communities everywhere.
